content: Folate, a B-vitamin, is essential for DNA synthesis, methylation, and cellular division. Wheat and maize flour, which are staple foods globally, have been fortified with folic acid in over 80 countries to prevent neural tube defects. Folic acid fortification is considered a potential strategy to improve folate levels and other health outcomes in populations. The objective of this review was to assess the health benefits and safety of fortifying wheat and maize flour with folic acid, either alone or in combination with other micronutrients, compared to unfortified flour or no intervention. The review included studies involving individuals over two years of age, including pregnant and lactating women, from various countries. The search for relevant studies was conducted in multiple databases up to May 2018, and additional searches for ongoing or planned studies were performed in June 2018. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-RCTs, and prospective observational studies with control groups were included. However, non-RCTs and observational studies were not included in meta-analyses but were described in terms of their characteristics and findings. A total of 10 studies were included in the review. Four studies provided data for quantitative analyses, five were RCTs, three were non-RCTs, and two were interrupted time series (ITS) studies. The studies were conducted in countries with varying income levels, including China, Mexico, South Africa, Bangladesh, and Canada. Seven studies examined wheat flour fortified with folic acid, while three focused on maize flour. The duration of interventions ranged from two weeks to 36 months, with ITS studies including post-fortification periods of up to seven years. Most studies had unclear risks of bias in randomization, blinding, and reporting, but low or unclear risks of bias for attrition and contamination. Regarding neural tube defects, none of the included RCTs reported this outcome. However, one non-RCT found that wheat flour fortified with folic acid and other micronutrients was associated with a significantly lower risk of total neural tube defects, spina bifida, and encephalocoele, but not anencephaly, compared to unfortified flour. The evidence for this finding was of low certainty. In terms of folate status, pregnant women who consumed folic acid-fortified maize porridge had significantly higher erythrocyte folate and plasma folate concentrations compared to those who received no intervention. However, women of reproductive age consuming maize flour fortified with folic acid and other micronutrients did not show higher erythrocyte or plasma folate levels compared to those consuming unfortified maize flour. Adults consuming folic acid-fortified wheat flour bread rolls had higher erythrocyte and plasma folate levels compared to those consuming unfortified flour. Additionally, two non-RCTs reported significantly higher serum folate concentrations among women consuming fortified flour compared to unfortified flour. For haemoglobin levels and anaemia, a cluster-randomized trial among children found no significant effects of fortified wheat flour flatbread on haemoglobin concentrations or anaemia compared to unfortified flatbread. The authors concluded that fortifying wheat flour with folic acid may reduce the risk of neural tube defects, although this outcome was only reported in one non-RCT. Fortification of wheat or maize flour with folic acid, either alone or with other micronutrients, may increase erythrocyte and serum/plasma folate concentrations. However, evidence is limited regarding the effects of folic acid-fortified flour on haemoglobin levels or anaemia. The effects of folic acid fortification on other primary outcomes remain unknown, and no studies reported adverse effects. The review was limited by the small number of studies and participants, study design limitations, and the low certainty of evidence due to the way the included studies were conducted and reported.
